newsitem.title: UK: UK FTSE ends at record close but short of new peak.
newsitem.headline: UK FTSE ends at record close but short of new peak.

text.p: London's FTSE 100 share index ended at a new record close on Tuesday but fell short of its all-time high as a dithering Dow took the steam out of a strong early rally in British leading shares.
The FTSE closed 50.6 points higher at 4,357.7, just beating the previous closing high set on February 19.
But it failed to breach its record peak of 4,362.4 and was stopped in its tracks just below the 4,360 level when an expected helping hand from the Dow failed to materialise.
"It was a very good day but Wall Street just didn't help us enough to take us to a new record," one dealer said.

Monday's turnaround by the Dow, which ended higher after three losing sessions, fired up the FTSE in morning trade. But Wall Street wavered on Tuesday, with the Dow swinging between modest gains and modest losses, restraining the FTSE's progress.
Dealers said the tone in London remained firm and a strong close on Wall Street would set up an assault on the FTSE's all-time highs.
"Volume wasn't spectacular today but we saw very few sellers," a trader said. "People don't seem interested in taking profits even on shares which have had a very strong run."
Volume on SEAQ was 781.4 million by 1700 GMT.

Dealers said expectations of further cash inflows from private investors were keeping British shares firm, with a month to go until the April deadline for investing in personal Equity Plans (PEPs), a tax-efficient means of investing in shares.

Wednesday sees the monthly monetary meeting between British Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George but analysts expect no change in interest rates and their attention is focused instead on events across the Atlantic.
Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan ends his Humphrey Hawkins testimony on Wednesday. Stocks dived last week when he warned Wall Street's rise "raised questions of sustainability".

In testimony to the U.S. House Budget Committee on Tuesday, Greenspan defended his comments, saying they were intended to explain monetary policy moves the Fed might undertake in the future rather than sway financial markets.
Analysts said the second half of his Humphrey Hawkins speech would be scrutinised for any hint that U.S. interest rates could rise. Some believe a March 25 rate hike cannot be ruled out.
Friday's U.S. February employment report will also be crucial for markets this week, analysts said.
Advancing stocks outnumbered decliners in the FTSE by more than four to one.
Best performer in the FTSE was Anglo-Australian conglomerate BTR Plc, which climbed 13p to 255-1/2 as investors snapped up stock ahead of its results on Thursday.

Smith & Nephew Plc was the weakest blue-chip, tumbling after chief executive John Robinson said bid talk surrounding the healthcare firm was baseless. The announcement of annual profits at the low-end of expectations also helped pull the stock lower. It ended seven pence off at 184.
Retailer MFI Furniture Group Plc took a battering after reporting a surprising slowdown in sales growth in the second half. It plunged 40-1/2p, or 20 percent, to 156-1/2.
MFI's gloomy news hit other household retailers -- Kingfisher Plc lost seven pence to 683-1/2 and Argos Plc ended 7-1/2p weaker at 685.
Northern-Ireland based engineering firm Mackie International Group Plc plummeted 51p or 28 percent to 132-1/2 after announcing that talks on a possible takeover bid had halted.

On the upside, building materials firm RMC Group Plc climbed 29p to 988, helped by bullish comments on the sector by Irish-based building firm CRH Plc, and Zeneca Group Plc rose 45-1/2p to 18.82 stg, rebounding from last week's losses.
-- Andrew Marshall, London newsroom +44 171 542 4026 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
